stories.headline: US Federal Reserve raises interest rates to 4% despite demands from Donald Trump
stories.body:
The US Federal Reserve raised its main interest rate on September 16, 2026. The central bank voted unanimously to approve the change. The vote increased the benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point. This rate now sits in a range between 3.75% and 4%.

US President Donald Trump demanded a rate cut after the decision. Trump said that interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh defended the rate hike. Warsh said that inflation is too high. He said that inflation has stayed high for too long.

The Federal Reserve targets an inflation rate of 2% or below. But US inflation has remained above that target for more than five years. US consumer price index inflation reached 3.4% in August 2026. The Federal Reserve also raised its inflation forecast for 2026. The central bank raised the forecast to 3.7%. Its previous projection was 3.6%.

White House senior deputy press secretary Kush Desai described the rate hike as unfortunate. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer also criticized the interest rate increase. Schumer said the hike will make everything more expensive. He blamed the economic management of Donald Trump.

Commercial banks moved quickly to adjust their rates after the announcement. Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp, and BNY raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday. The banks pushed the rate to 7% from 6.75%.

Yields on 10-year US Treasury bonds rose past the 5% threshold after the rate hike announcement.

A majority of Federal Reserve policymakers expect interest rates to be hiked again. They expect another increase before the end of 2026. They project the rate will end up between 4% and 4.25%.

In other action, the US Congress passed new legislation. Lawmakers passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in a 262 to 159 vote.

stories.headline: Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca as regional tensions escalate
stories.body:
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen's Houthi rebels of launching a drone attack toward Mecca. Saudi forces intercepted the attempted attack. Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said the security of the Two Holy Mosques and pilgrims is a red line.

Houthi forces released a video claiming to show a Saudi fighter jet shot down in Marib Governorate. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed their forces shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet. Saree said they used a locally made air-to-air missile over Marib province.

Saudi Arabia shut down its East-West pipeline after an attack by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. Global crude oil prices remain above $100 a barrel.

US officials held meetings with Houthi leaders over the weekend at the US embassy in Muscat, Oman. Houthi leaders assured US officials that their 2025 ceasefire holds. They said they will not target US shipping in the Red Sea. Suez Canal earnings fell by about $6 billion in 2024 due to Red Sea security disruptions.

stories.headline: European Union proposes associate membership for Canada in key speech
stories.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed associate membership for Canada in the European Union. She made the proposal during her State of the Union address on September 16, 2026. Canada would become the first associate member of the European Union under the proposal.

Canada is currently the only non-European country allowed into a major European defense program. The country can participate in the European Union's 150-billion-euro fund for joint defense purchases. Canada spends 2% of its gross domestic product on defense. The nation committed with NATO partners to raise total defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035.

Ten of the 27 European Union member states have not yet ratified the free-trade agreement with Canada.

Ursula von der Leyen made other key proposals during her speech. She proposed creating a European Security Council including the United Kingdom and Ukraine. She also proposed a ban on social media platforms for children under 13 across the European Union.

Canada spends 2% of its GDP on defense and has committed with NATO partners to increase total defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035.

stories.headline: Hague tribunal sentences former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi to 25 years for war crimes
stories.body:
The Specialist Court in The Hague found former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi guilty of war crimes. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers sentenced Thaçi and former Kosovo Liberation Army leader Jakup Krasniqi to 25 years in prison each. The court sentenced former KLA leaders Kadri Veseli to 18 years and Rexhep Selimi to 13 years.

Judges convicted Thaçi and his co-defendants of arbitrary detention of 385 people. The court found them guilty of cruel treatment of 49 people and torture of 303 detainees. They were also convicted of the murder of 96 people.

Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti called the convictions and sentences an unacceptable injustice. Dutch riot police detained two people after clashes with Thaçi supporters outside the court. The 1998-1999 Kosovo War left about 13,000 people dead, including about 9,000 ethnic Albanian Kosovars.

In Sweden's election, the left-leaning opposition is projected to win 176 seats in parliament compared to 173 for the governing coalition and Sweden Democrats.

stories.headline: US lawmaker places hold on $2.8 billion arms package to Israel
stories.body:
US Representative Gregory Meeks placed a hold on a proposed $2.8 billion arms transfer to Israel. The proposed weapons package includes 20,000 MK-84 bombs. It also includes 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared a national security emergency in 2025. That declaration bypassed congressional review to fast-track nearly $3 billion in weapons sales to Israel.

The Biden administration paused a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in 2024. Donald Trump reversed that decision after taking office in January 2025.

Opposition to military support for Israel has grown among some lawmakers in Washington. More than 100 House Democrats voted in July 2026 to end US military assistance to Israel.

stories.headline: Damaged buildings collapse in Gaza, killing dozens of residents
stories.body:
A war-damaged building collapsed in Gaza City's Tal al-Hawa area, killing at least 21 people. The six-story building had been damaged by a prior Israeli strike. Eight children were among those killed in the collapse.

Another war-damaged seven-story building collapsed in Gaza, killing at least 20 people. Nine members of Hayat al-Ajlah's extended family died when the al-Saada building collapsed in western Gaza City.

United Nations Development Programme Gaza head Alessandro Mrakic issued a warning about structural dangers. Mrakic warned that around 400 war-damaged buildings across Gaza face imminent risk of collapse.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said 70% of Gaza's population was emptied from homes during the military offensive. More than 73,790 people have been killed in Gaza since October 7, 2023, according to Gaza's health ministry. The ministry reported that 1,369 Palestinians were killed and 4,627 wounded since the ceasefire took effect on October 11, 2025.

stories.headline: Pakistani corvette collides with Indian warship in Arabian Sea, triggering protests
stories.body:
A Pakistani naval corvette collided with an Indian warship in the North Arabian Sea on September 15, 2026. The incident occurred in the evening involving Pakistan Navy vessel PNS Hunain. The Pakistani ship hit a frontline Indian Navy warship.

The collision caused different levels of damage to the two vessels. PNS Hunain sustained damage during the impact. The Pakistani corvette returned to harbour after the collision. The Indian vessel suffered minor damage. It continued its routine surveillance mission.

A source told the Times of India about the actions of the Indian commander. The source said the captain of the Indian warship exercised extreme restraint to prevent a severe accident.

Both countries lodged formal diplomatic protests following the collision. The Indian Ministry of External Affairs summoned Pakistan's Chargé d'Affaires in New Delhi. India delivered a strong diplomatic protest over the incident.

India claimed the Pakistani ship broke a long-standing military agreement. The Ministry of External Affairs said the Pakistani vessel violated Article 10 of a 1991 pact. That agreement is the Agreement on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements. Article 10 mandates that naval ships and submarines maintain a distance of at least three nautical miles. The rule aims to prevent accidents in international waters.

Pakistan also lodged a diplomatic protest over the collision. Pakistan's foreign ministry summoned Indian Chargé d'Affaires Satyanjal Pandey late on Wednesday night. Pakistan summoned the diplomat in Islamabad. Pakistani officials called the collision a highly provocative action. They said the incident occurred inside Pakistan's exclusive economic zone.

PNS Hunain is a Yarmook-class offshore patrol vessel. Damen Shipyards built the vessel in Romania. The Pakistan Navy commissioned the ship in July 2024.

This collision marks the first reported military incident between the two nations since May 2025. That earlier period involved four days of hostilities following the Pahalgam terror attack. The last recorded collision between warships of the two nations occurred in June 2011. During that incident, PNS Babur touched INS Godavari during an anti-piracy patrol in the Gulf of Aden.

PNS Hunain sustained damage in the collision and returned to harbour, while the Indian vessel suffered minor damage and continued its routine surveillance mission.
A source told the Times of India that the captain of the Indian warship exercised extreme restraint to prevent a severe accident.

The Indian Ministry of External Affairs stated that the Pakistani naval ship's conduct violated Article 10 of the April 1991 bilateral Agreement on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements.

Article 10 of the 1991 agreement between India and Pakistan mandates that naval ships and submarines maintain a distance of at least three nautical miles from each other to avoid accidents in international waters.

stories.headline: Indian government rules out rollback of 0.4% UPI merchant transaction charges
stories.body:
The Union government ruled out any rollback of new charges on digital payments. A 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate will apply to UPI merchant payments of ₹2,000 or more. The government set the start date for October 15, 2026. The fee is capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month through UPI QR payments are excluded. Merchant transactions up to Rs 2,000 and all person-to-person transfers remain free. Capital market payments will face a 0.02% rate capped at ₹300, while specified essential sectors face a flat ₹5 charge.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi criticized Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the policy. Gandhi called the framework a UPI tax. Five Congress MPs served on the parliamentary committee that recommended the framework. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance presented its report on August 12, 2026. The committee adopted the report without recorded dissent.

Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah backed the decision. Abdullah said operating digital payment infrastructure is costly. Abdullah noted person-to-person money transfers carry no charge.

Legal and retail challenges have emerged. Advocate Anjan Datta filed a public interest litigation in the Supreme Court to stop the framework. Retailers Association of India CEO Kumar Rajagopalan said small merchants will think twice about accepting cash or UPI. The Clothing Manufacturers Association of India expressed concern over extra pressure during the festive season.
